claims.claim: On make_classification data with 2.4% positives, all-negative accuracy was 0.976, logistic regression at 0.5 had recall 0.0, average precision 0.30 against a random 0.025.
claims.source: Run with scikit-learn 1.8.0 and 1.9.1 in this repository (random_state=0).

concept_html:
A metric is a summary of the mistakes you care about. Choose it from the decision the model supports, before you train anything.

Accuracy fails on imbalanced data. A test set from this course's build has 2.4% positives. Predicting "negative" for everyone scores accuracy 0.976. A logistic regression at the default 0.5 threshold scored 0.9755, with recall 0.0: it found no positives at all.

Better summaries, all in scikit-learn 1.8:

  • ROC AUC (roc_auc_score): the chance a random positive ranks above a random negative. It ignores the threshold and the class balance. Good for comparing rankers. It hides how many false positives come with each true positive when positives are rare.
  • Average precision, the area under the precision-recall curve (average_precision_score): sensitive to rare positives. A random ranking scores the prevalence, 0.025 here. The same logistic regression scored 0.30, twelve times the baseline. Always quote the baseline next to it.
  • Precision and recall at a threshold: precision is the share of flagged cases that are real. Recall is the share of real cases that are flagged. These map straight onto work: "of 100 customers we call, 30 were going to churn" and "we reach 64% of the churners".
  • Cost-weighted metrics: if a missed fraud costs £400 and a false alarm costs £5 of analyst time, compute the total cost at each threshold and pick the cheapest.

Pick the threshold from the decision too. 0.5 is a default of the library, not a business rule. If the team can review 200 cases a day, the threshold is whatever flags 200 cases.

Report the metric with the prevalence and the number of positives in the test set. A precision of 0.30 from 12 positives is not the same evidence as from 1,200.

lines: import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score
def evaluate(y_true: np.ndarray, scores: np.ndarray, threshold: float) -> dict[str, float | None]:
"""Ranking and threshold metrics, with the baseline to compare against."""
flagged = scores >= threshold
tp = int((flagged & (y_true == 1)).sum())
n_flagged, n_pos = int(flagged.sum()), int((y_true == 1).sum())
return {
"prevalence": float(y_true.mean()),
"roc_auc": float(roc_auc_score(y_true, scores)),
"average_precision": float(average_precision_score(y_true, scores)),
"precision": tp / n_flagged if n_flagged > 0 else None,
"recall": tp / n_pos if n_pos > 0 else None,
}

exercises.solution:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score


def evaluate(y_true: np.ndarray, scores: np.ndarray, threshold: float) -> dict[str, float | None]:
    """Ranking metrics, threshold metrics and the prevalence baseline.

    Args:
        y_true: Binary labels.
        scores: Model scores, higher means more likely positive.
        threshold: Flag cases with score >= threshold.

    Returns:
        prevalence, roc_auc, average_precision, precision, recall.
    """
    flagged = scores >= threshold
    tp = int((flagged & (y_true == 1)).sum())
    n_flagged = int(flagged.sum())
    n_pos = int((y_true == 1).sum())
    return {
        "prevalence": float(y_true.mean()),
        "roc_auc": float(roc_auc_score(y_true, scores)),
        "average_precision": float(average_precision_score(y_true, scores)),
        "precision": tp / n_flagged if n_flagged > 0 else None,
        "recall": tp / n_pos if n_pos > 0 else None,
    }

title: Choose the metric from the decision
why_html: A claims triage model was reported as "97.6% accurate". It flagged nothing. Fraud prevalence was 2.4%, so a model that approved every claim scored the same. The number went into a board paper before anyone asked how many frauds it caught. The answer was zero.
